scope: One consecutive record; full stored text, registered 1280x720 native/mobile image, side-income earnings-claim, tax-treatment, internal-arithmetic and Mary-ledger capital checks

title.analysis: '15 Low Effort Boring Tasks That Make More Than Your Job' stacks a numbered list (15), two effort-reducing adjectives (Low Effort, Boring) and a comparative income promise (Make More Than Your Job). The comparative is the strongest and riskiest element: it is an implied earnings claim against the viewer's own salary, with no qualifier such as 'can' or 'eventually'. It has no dollar figure, which the channel's stronger income titles use. Same-channel comparisons: the closest structural sibling, 5UiyM5UGEes '10 LAZY Money Habits That Build Quiet Wealth' 0.9092x TYPICAL, and 5x_qbbMPNq0 'It's Boring, But It Will Make You Richer Than Anyone You Know' 1.40215x TYPICAL show that 'lazy/boring' framing lands in the TYPICAL band on this channel. Titles with a concrete monthly dollar threshold do better: HWU9IQB9Q-k 'Why Everything Changes After $1K Month Passive Income' 2.27303x STRONG, vdMkNfJYqLI 'The 3 Passive Income Milestones That Change Everything' 2.00183x STRONG, UfqNzF7sQzo '$3,000 Month Passive Income' 1.6745x TYPICAL, and xtdEdCdznsg 'How To Turn $10,000 Into $500,000 (The Lazy Method)' 2.18248x STRONG, which pairs 'lazy' with a dollar transformation. A list of income options without a dollar anchor, 1JynDORGRis '12 High Paying Jobs That Don't Need a Degree' 1.11497x TYPICAL, sits mid-band, and the explainer counterexample uSZ1N2ZAmDM 'Dividends 101' 0.3188x WEAK shows that the investing items in this video are not a strong standalone draw. Descriptive pattern across eight titles: dollar-anchored passive-income titles co-occur with stronger ratios than effort-adjective lists; not a proven cause.
title.search_demand: Moderate generic search intent around 'passive income ideas' and 'side hustles'; the exact phrase 'boring tasks that make more than your job' is not a typical query, so most demand is likely browse/suggested. Historical query volume and traffic sources unavailable.
title.script_alignment: Partially aligned. The script delivers exactly 15 numbered items, so the count is honest. 'Low effort' is contradicted by the script's own caveats: vending machines require cold calling building managers, digital downloads need '20 to 40 hours a week for the first few months', print on demand is a multi-year back catalog, car washes and laundromats break 'on schedules they set for themselves', and fewer than 5% of laundromats run without the owner. 'Make More Than Your Job' is not delivered: the narrator's own composite example, Mary, ends at 'just over $1,300 a month' (about $15,600 a year) against a $58,000 salary and $3,400 monthly take-home (about $40,800 a year, analyst calculation). Only the laundromat item ($40,000 to $100,000 net for an active owner, after a roughly $320,000 leveraged purchase) approaches a salary, and it is neither low effort nor a 'task'. Items 6 to 10 (savings, T-bills, dividend and REIT funds, real estate lending) are investments whose income scales with capital, not tasks.

thumbnail.analysis: Registered maxresdefault fetched fresh and inspected at native 1280x720 and proportional 320x180. White background. Across the full top: very large black condensed uppercase text '15 LAZY INCOME STREAMS'; the character's head overlaps and hides most of the letters 'LA' in 'LAZY', so the word reads as '15 _ZY' at a glance and is recognizable mainly from context. Left: a cartoon man with a large egg-shaped head, half-lidded eyes, smug closed-mouth smile and prominent chin, white rolled-sleeve shirt and blue trousers, pointing right with his index finger; a thick black curved arrow below his arm also points right. The character's design closely resembles the Peter Griffin character from Family Guy; whether this raises any rights issue is not assessed here. Right: a 3x2 grid of colored circular icons with bold black labels: red laptop with rising chart 'AFFILIATE', blue open book 'EBOOKS', green camera 'STOCK PHOTOS', yellow house 'AIRBNB', orange car with dollar coin 'CAR RENTAL', purple falling coins 'DIVIDENDS'. Hierarchy: headline text, then the character's face, then the bright icon grid via the pointing finger and arrow. At 320px the headline remains legible apart from the occluded 'LA'; the six icons stay distinguishable by color but the labels shrink to roughly 5 to 6 pixel tall text and become hard to read; the facial expression still reads as smug. Packaging-to-script mismatch: four of the six labeled streams (Affiliate, Ebooks, Airbnb, Car Rental) do not appear among the script's 15 items, which are parking, storage, vending, ATMs, car wash, savings, T-bills/I bonds, dividend funds, REITs, real estate lending, digital downloads, print on demand, stock photos/video, focus groups and laundromats. Only 'STOCK PHOTOS' and 'DIVIDENDS' match. The thumbnail also says 'INCOME STREAMS' while the title says 'Boring Tasks', and neither the image nor the title shows the script's strongest hook (Jude and Mary, same $58,000 salary, $190 versus $1,240). Historical continuity, A/B testing and CTR contribution are unverified.

script.opening_words: Jude and Mary grew up in the same neighborhood, went to the same state school, graduated the same year.
script.ending_words: I'm not a financial advisor and nothing here is financial advice. If this was useful, subscribe and I'll keep making these. See you in the next one.
script.analysis: Full 20,047 canonical characters read in three contiguous chunks (0-10,000, 10,000-20,000, 20,000-20,047). The hook is a controlled comparison story: Jude and Mary share neighborhood, school, graduation year, a roughly $58,000 salary and $3,400 monthly take-home, then diverge on the same Tuesday, Jude with '$190 left and 3 weeks until the next paycheck' and Mary with '$1,240 that came in this month' from 'boring, unsexy systems'. This is the strongest writing in the video: it holds every variable constant except the one the video sells, uses concrete dollar amounts and a specific day, and pre-empts the 'he just overspends' objection ('No shopping addiction, no gambling problem, the money just goes'). The intro then makes the promise ('15 of the most boring, low-effort income tasks that can quietly make you more than your job'), softening the title with 'can'. A tax-and-inflation section frames one paycheck as structurally disadvantaged before Mary returns as a bridge ('Here's exactly how she did it'), which converts the thesis into a case study. Items are delivered in a consistent micro-template: what it is, a dollar range, startup cost, time, then an 'honest note' caveat. That template is the script's best technique, because the caveats (vault cash 'literally sitting inside a metal box in someone else's bar', 'absentee ownership' called misleading, only '15 to 25% of designs generate any sales', AI pressure on stock photos) build credibility. Mary is threaded through items 1, 2 and 14 as a running example, and section signposts ('Five down, 10 to go', the pivot 'Everything so far requires space you own or equipment you buy. The next five require neither', '10 down, five left') keep the 15-item length navigable; the pivot is the most effective transition because it explains why the list changes category. The mid-video re-engagement ('Most watch a video like this, feel briefly motivated, and go back') is a standard pattern interrupt that flatters the remaining viewer. Weaknesses: the honest caveats directly undercut the 'low effort' and 'more than your job' promise, so the packaging and the content disagree; several internal numbers contradict each other (vending, print on demand, Mary's monthly total); and the closing Mary ledger quietly requires about $160,000 of invested capital, which a $58,000 earner could not have accumulated in 18 months from salary, so the hook's 'same salary' premise is broken at the payoff. The close returns to the Jude/Mary frame ('Jude is still waiting. Mary already stopped thinking about it'), gives three concrete 15-to-45-minute actions (open a high-yield account, list a parking or storage space, start SCHD or VNQ in a Roth IRA with $50 a month), then a not-financial-advice disclaimer and subscribe call to action; the early subscribe/like ask also appears at about 1,500 characters. No sponsor, affiliate link or paid product appears in the stored text; the video description was not reviewed. All stored text read; not an original-audio, editing or retention verification.

claim_audit: Title and promise 'make more than your job' versus the script's own numbers: Mary's combined result is 'just over $1,300 a month', about $15,600 a year, against a stated $3,400 monthly take-home, about $40,800 a year (analyst calculation, 38%). Most item ranges (parking $150 to $360, storage $160 to $400, savings interest, focus groups $150 to $900 a month) are a fraction of a $58,000 salary. In FTC terms, presenting outlier examples (Boston host over $1,000 a month, Rachel Jimenez $110,000 in year two, Amoro Designs $93,000 a year, a laundromat owner at about $2 million across four locations) without typical-result context resembles the atypical-earnings pattern that FTC consent orders (for example the Lurn/Singal and Cohen orders) require advertisers to pair with clear disclosure of typical customer results. This video sells no product in its stored text, so FTC rules on sellers do not directly apply; the point is that the claims would not meet that standard. The script partly mitigates this with honest caveats and once gives a median (Etsy median profit $489 versus $2,444 average revenue).

Mary ledger capital: $40,000 in high-yield savings earning $1,680 a year implies 4.2% APY (analyst calculation, plausible). 'SCHD in her Roth IRA paying $340 in dividends last quarter' at the video's own 3.4% yield implies about $40,000 in SCHD (340 x 4 / 0.034). Known items total about $638 a month (195 + 190 + 140 + 113), so 'just over $1,300' requires about $662 a month from Groundfloor, about $81,000 lent at 9.8%. Total implied capital is about $161,000 (analyst calculation). That is incompatible with the hook's premise of a $58,000 earner with $3,400 take-home building this in 18 months from 'four evenings' of setup, and $40,000 in a Roth IRA in 18 months exceeds IRS annual contribution limits ($7,000 for 2025, $7,500 for 2026; limits stated from analyst knowledge, not re-fetched here) unless funded by rollover or conversion. The opening figure ($1,240 a month) and the closing figure (just over $1,300) also differ, and the closing list omits the dividend deposit and focus-group income in a consistent way. Also the $340 is an annual figure for $10,000 in item 8 but a quarterly figure for Mary, which may be a script slip.

Vending internal contradiction: 'Average net profit per machine, $300 to $600 a month' but 'A 10-machine operation produces $500 to $1,200 a month'. Ten machines at the stated per-machine figure would be $3,000 to $6,000 a month (analyst calculation); the two figures cannot both hold. Neither figure is sourced.

Print-on-demand internal contradiction: 'roughly $1 per active design per month' then '100 designs, $300 a month'. At $1 per design, 100 designs is $100 a month; '500 designs ... $3,000 to $5,000 a month' implies $6 to $10 per design (analyst calculation). The stated '15 to 25% of designs generate any sales' further lowers the per-design average. Unsourced.

Tax thesis: 'If that same dollar came from a dividend, a long-term investment, or rental income stream, it gets taxed at a completely different, much lower, rate' and 'every additional one gets more favorable treatment' is wrong for most of the video's own list. Net rental income, high-yield savings interest, T-bill and I bond interest (federally), most REIT dividends (the script itself says so), Groundfloor interest, vending, ATM, car wash and laundromat profits, Etsy, print-on-demand, stock royalties and focus-group pay are taxed as ordinary income, and self-employment business income adds 15.3% self-employment tax. Only qualified dividends and long-term capital gains get the 0 to 20% rates (plus the 3.8% net investment income tax at higher incomes, not mentioned). The script contradicts its own thesis at item 9.

'The Forbes 400 wealthiest Americans paid an average effective tax rate of 8.2%': matches the 2021 White House CEA/OMB estimate of an 8.2% average federal individual income tax rate for the 400 wealthiest families over 2010 to 2018, available well before publication. The narrator omits that the estimate counts unrealized gains on unsold assets as income, which is why it is low; the comparison 'most middle-class workers pay more than double that' is not sourced and mixes income tax with the payroll tax mentioned earlier.

'The IRS data on millionaires shows they average seven income streams' (repeated in the close): no primary IRS document was found; search results show only secondary commentary repeating the figure and articles describing it as a myth with an unclear origin. Treat as UNVERIFIED and likely misattributed; the causal explanation ('because the first income stream gets taxed the hardest') is narrator opinion.

Take-home on $58,000: analyst calculation for a single 2026 filer (standard deduction $16,100; 10% and 12% brackets) gives federal income tax about $4,780 plus 7.65% FICA about $4,437, leaving about $48,783 before state tax; a 5% to 6% state income tax brings that near $45,500 to $46,000, so the narrator's $42,000 to $46,000 range is plausible for income-tax states but understates no-income-tax states. The hook's '$3,400 a month after taxes' ($40,800 a year) falls below the narrator's own range unless pre-tax benefits or retirement contributions are deducted; minor internal inconsistency. 2026 bracket parameters are analyst knowledge, not re-fetched.

I bonds '4.03% composite': consistent with the November 2025 to April 2026 rate (0.90% fixed, 4.03% composite) shown on TreasuryDirect's rate page and secondary coverage, current at the 2026-04-12 publication. Omitted: the $10,000 annual electronic purchase limit, a 12-month lockup and a 3-month interest penalty before five years. The state and local tax exemption for T-bill and I bond interest is correct.

High-yield savings: '0.39% national average' and '10 to 12 times more' (implying about 3.9% to 4.7%) are plausible but were not checked against the FDIC national-rate page for April 2026; UNVERIFIED. '$10,000 ... could earn enough to cover a utility bill or your internet every month': at 4.2%, $10,000 earns about $35 a month (analyst calculation), below most monthly internet bills; overstated.

SCHD: '$10,000 generates roughly $340 a year, $28 a month' is correct at 3.4% ($28.33). '$340 this year becomes $378 next year' implies 11.2% growth; '$800 annually' in 10 years requires about 9% annual dividend growth without reinvestment ($805) or more with reinvestment ($1,232 at 10% growth plus 3.4% reinvestment; analyst calculations). Yield, the 12% ten-year return and the 10 to 14% dividend growth rate were not verified for April 2026; past growth is not a forecast.

REITs: the 90% taxable-income distribution requirement is correct. 'VNQ ... across 150 plus commercial properties' likely conflates holdings with properties: the fund holds REIT securities (each owning many properties); not verified here. 'Hold them inside a Roth IRA or 401k, and the tax drag disappears entirely' is true for Roth accounts but not for a traditional 401(k), where withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income (tax deferred, not removed).

Car wash: 'Self-service locations generate $50,000 to $100,000 in annual revenue at 14.6% net margins' implies $7,300 to $14,600 a year net, about $608 to $1,217 a month (analyst calculation), after buying a location from about $50,000; this is far from 'more than your job'. The KKR $850 million Quick Quack investment concerns an express-tunnel subscription chain, not self-service bays; the deal amount was not verified here.

Laundromat: '94.8% five-year survival' versus 'Restaurants sit around 60%' is unsourced and UNVERIFIED (the 94.8% figure appears to come from industry marketing, not BLS business-survival data). SBA arithmetic is internally consistent: 10% down of $32,000 implies a $320,000 purchase, and $80,000 a year on $320,000 is 25%, within the stated 20 to 28% ROI. But on a $288,000 loan at an assumed 10% over 10 years, debt service is about $3,806 a month or $45,671 a year (analyst calculation, rate and term assumed), leaving about $34,329 before owner labor, repairs and taxes if $80,000 is profit; if $80,000 is revenue the deal does not cover debt service. 'Dave Mens' is probably an ASR rendering of the Laundromat Millionaire's name; not corrected. '$2 million annually' is unclear between revenue and earnings; UNVERIFIED.

Etsy '164,000 digital shops ... average monthly revenue of $2,444, median profit around $489', 'Rachel Jimenez hit $110,000', 'Amoro Designs earns $93,000', 'Neighbor reports hosts average $294 per hour', 'Groundfloor ... around 10% since 2013', 'video earns roughly 20 times more per clip', 'Prolific averages $12.50 an hour', 'self-storage industry generates over $40 billion' and 'essentials ... surged by nearly 25% ... wage growth ... 21%' since 2021: no source named in the script and not checked in this review; UNVERIFIED. The $2,444 mean versus $489 median gap itself signals a skewed distribution where a typical shop earns far less than the headline.

Internally consistent arithmetic checked: ATM 300 x $3 = $900 gross; Groundfloor $5,000 across 50 x $100 loans; VNQ $10,000 x 3.85% = $385; Neighbor $160 for 30 minutes is about $320 per hour, roughly consistent with the $294 claim. Focus groups: three '60 to 90-minute' groups total 3 to 4.5 hours, not 'six hours' (analyst calculation); minor.

Possible ASR artefacts preserved, not corrected against audio: 'Dave Mens' (likely a name misrendering), 'Spacer' (likely Spacer or Spacer.com), 'ground-floor account' (likely Groundfloor), and 'four bags of groceries less'.

topic.analysis: Side income and passive income listicle mixing three categories: asset rentals (parking, storage), small cash-business ownership (vending, ATM, car wash, laundromat), capital-yield products (savings, T-bills, I bonds, SCHD, VNQ, Groundfloor) and creator or gig income (digital downloads, print on demand, stock media, focus groups). Evergreen; beginner audience; very high household relevance because it addresses 'my paycheck runs out' anxiety. Distinctive audience question: 'What can I set up once that pays me without a second job?' The answer is broad but uneven, because a $10 Groundfloor loan and a $320,000 leveraged laundromat are presented as the same kind of 'boring task'.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Original opportunity: keep the Jude/Mary controlled comparison but make Mary's ledger arithmetically honest (show the capital each stream needs and how long a $58,000 earner takes to accumulate it), sort items by required capital and hours rather than presenting 15 equal options, and attach typical rather than outlier earnings with a named source for each number. A tax-accurate version (which streams are ordinary income, which carry self-employment tax, which get qualified-dividend rates) would directly correct the most common error in this genre.

virality.analysis: Observed result: 6,609 frozen views at 151.1351 days; ten-peer ratio 0.59678x TYPICAL and five-peer ratio 0.66659x TYPICAL, both independently reproduced; the tier agrees across peer windows but sits in the lower part of the TYPICAL band, about 0.1 above the WEAK boundary. Likes 289 (4.37% of views) and comments 46 (0.70%). Evidence-backed interpretation: among its ten age peers, the two STRONG videos carry concrete self-comparison or object hooks ('15 Signs You Are Actually Doing Better Than the Average Person' 2.18459x, 'Why Everything Changes After Paying Off Your Car Loan' 3.43336x), and the channel's dollar-anchored passive-income titles (HWU9IQB9Q-k 2.27303x, vdMkNfJYqLI 2.00183x, xtdEdCdznsg 2.18248x) outperform this effort-adjective list; this is a descriptive pattern only. Hypotheses: (a) the title's comparative 'more than your job' promise without a dollar figure may read as generic side-hustle content, a crowded genre; (b) the thumbnail's icon grid advertises streams (Affiliate, Ebooks, Airbnb, Car Rental) not in the video, and its 320px labels are hard to read, so packaging may neither stand out nor match; (c) the relatively high like rate may indicate viewers who clicked found the specific, caveated delivery useful, a possible packaging-not-content gap. Proposed experiment: in owned uploads, test the same script under a dollar-anchored title using the honest outcome (for example 'How a $58K Earner Built $1,300 a Month in Side Income') and a thumbnail that shows the script's actual items, versus an effort-adjective title, and measure CTR, impressions, 30-second retention and retention across the item-6 category pivot. None of these hypotheses is measurable here without impressions, CTR, traffic sources or retention.

Confounders: algorithmic exploration timing, competition from the channel's own STRONG uploads that week, unknown later title/thumbnail edits.

original_content_lesson.test: Produce a side-income list where every earnings figure is a typical or median value with a named source, Mary-style composite examples are arithmetically reconciled with the stated salary and timeline, and tax treatment per stream is stated; test dollar-anchored honest packaging against effort-adjective packaging in owned experiments and measure CTR, retention at the category pivot, and comment sentiment about credibility.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH for stored-text internal contradictions (vending, print on demand, Mary ledger capital) and tax-treatment errors; MEDIUM for the dollar-anchored versus effort-adjective descriptive pattern; LOW for causal virality attribution.
